mechanism: Mostly contact. Landing on another player's foot in traffic (rebounds, contested shots, drives into a crowded lane) forces the ankle into inversion. Non-contact cases come from cutting on a fatigued or previously sprained ankle.
prevention: Lace-up bracing or taping, especially for players with a prior sprain|Sport-specific balance/proprioception work 3x per week (single-leg catches, landings on unstable surfaces)|Finish rehab to full single-leg hop and balance symmetry before return, not just pain-free|Coach defenders to contest vertically rather than sliding under a shooter's landing zone
monitoring: Flag every player with a sprain in the last 12 months|Single-leg balance and hop tests at preseason and after each sprain|Track minor 'day-to-day' sprains, since they predict the next one

mechanism: NBA ACL tears are mostly indirect contact or non-contact: the first explosive step toward the basket, landing after contact in the air, or a jump stop. The knee caves inward (valgus) within a few hundredths of a second of foot strike. Patellar tendon pain and meniscus injuries come from repetitive jumping load.
prevention: Neuromuscular warm-ups that train landing and deceleration: two-foot landings, knee over toes, hip and trunk control|Hip abductor/external rotator and hamstring strength to resist inward collapse|Deceleration drills for jump stops and first-step drives|Progressive jump-load planning for players with patellar tendon pain
monitoring: Video screen landings and cuts for valgus at preseason and mid-season|Watch for knee 'soreness' entries clustering in one player, often the early sign of tendon overload|Limb-symmetry strength and hop testing before return

mechanism: Almost always non-contact: a push-off or first step from a standstill, landing on the forefoot as the ankle snaps up into dorsiflexion while the knee straightens. Veterans, recent workload rises, and a recent calf strain on the same leg recur in the cases.
prevention: Eccentric and heavy calf-Achilles loading year-round (slow heel drops, weighted calf raises)|Lumbopelvic and knee stability work so the calf isn't absorbing the whole push-off|Graded, criteria-based return after any calf strain: objective calf strength and hop benchmarks before full intensity|Re-conditioning blocks after long layoffs before playoff-level minutes
monitoring: Treat any calf strain or Achilles 'soreness' as a red flag for the following weeks|Flag minutes running well above a player's season norm over the last 10-15 games|Extra caution for veterans and early-season or post-layoff ramps

mechanism: High-speed running and sudden acceleration, such as transition sprints and chasing a loose ball, stretch the hamstring while it is working to brake the leg.
prevention: Nordic hamstring exercise program (eccentric strength)|Sprint exposure in practice so game-speed running isn't a shock|Progress back to full-speed sprinting before clearing a strained player
monitoring: Eccentric hamstring strength testing (left-right asymmetry)|Watch guards and slashers in heavy transition stretches

mechanism: Bone stress injuries (fifth metatarsal, navicular) from repetitive loading, clustering in the first weeks of the season. Plantar fascia problems come from the same overload.
prevention: Gradual preseason ramp of court time and jumping volume|Footwear and orthotic review for high-load players|Early imaging for any persistent midfoot or lateral foot pain instead of playing through it
monitoring: Weekly jump and court-time load in the first 6 weeks|Treat 'sore foot' entries in big men as possible stress reactions

mechanism: Lateral cuts, defensive slides and sudden direction changes overload the adductors and hip flexors.
prevention: Copenhagen adductor strengthening program in-season|Hip mobility and lateral-movement prep before games
monitoring: Squeeze-test adductor strength regularly and after groin complaints
